sources.entry: OpenWA ⚠ - WhatsApp API gateway exposing messaging as REST endpoints, with a web dashboard, multi-account sessions, and webhook events (alternative to WhatsApp Business API providers). (Source Code, Clients) MIT Docker

summary.one_liner: OpenWA is a self-hosted, MIT-licensed WhatsApp API gateway that exposes messaging as REST endpoints, with a bundled web dashboard, multi-session support, and webhooks.
summary.what_it_does: It connects to WhatsApp through reverse-engineered clients (whatsapp-web.js by default, or @whiskeysockets/baileys selected via ENGINE_TYPE), not Meta's official Cloud API. It runs multiple WhatsApp sessions on one instance and exposes send, media, group, contact, label, channel and profile operations over HTTP, with Swagger docs. A React dashboard manages sessions, webhooks and API keys, and webhooks deliver events with HMAC signatures and optional filters. API keys have admin, operator and viewer roles that can be scoped to specific sessions or chats. An opt-in MCP endpoint lets AI agents call a curated set of tools. Storage can be SQLite or PostgreSQL, and local disk or S3/MinIO for media, with Redis optional for queues and rate limits.
use_cases: send WhatsApp messages from an application via REST API
run multiple WhatsApp accounts from one server
receive WhatsApp events via webhooks for automation
connect WhatsApp to n8n or other workflow tools
give an AI agent scoped access to WhatsApp chats
send OTPs, order updates or support replies from a backend
how_to_run: Alternative local dev: npm ci && npm run dev
notable: Pluggable adapters for database (SQLite/PostgreSQL) and storage (Local/S3) set through config
Session-scoped and chat-scoped API keys, including an allowlist of specific groups and contacts for shared accounts
Built-in MCP server with 26 read-only tools by default, or 52 with write tools
Webhook smart pre-dispatch filters on fields such as sender, chatId, body and type
Docker socket proxy sidecar and non-root container execution in the production setup
caveats: Unofficial, reverse-engineered WhatsApp clients carry a real risk of account restriction or ban; the README recommends dedicated numbers and not for regulated or compliance-sensitive use, where it advises Meta's official Cloud API.
whatsapp-web.js needs roughly 300-500 MB RAM per session; baileys needs about 30-80 MB but is described as easier for WhatsApp to fingerprint.
Some accounts cannot link a new device because of a WhatsApp passkey step, and the README says no OpenWA setting fixes this. Some features, such as call.received, are not reliable on whatsapp-web.js.
